title: Chapter 11 — Peculiar Effects Of The Love Of Physical Gratifications In Democratic Ages
paragraphs: From what has just been said, one might suppose that the love of physical gratifications must constantly drive the Americans into moral disorder, disturb the peace of families and threaten the security of society as a whole. That is not the case. In democracies the passion for physical gratifications has very different effects from those it has in aristocratic nations. Sometimes an aristocracy grows weary of public affairs and glutted with wealth. Amid the ruin of religious belief and the decline of the state, its heart may be gradually seduced into pursuing nothing but sensual pleasure. At other times the power of the monarch or the weakness of the people forces the nobility to keep away from the administration of affairs, without taking away their fortunes. With the road to great undertakings closed, they are left to the restlessness of their own desires. They then fall heavily back on themselves and look to bodily pleasures to forget their former greatness. When the members of an aristocratic body devote themselves entirely to physical gratifications in this way, they usually pour into that pursuit all the energy they have drawn from their long experience of power. Such men are not satisfied with the pursuit of comfort. They demand sumptuous depravity and splendid corruption. The worship they offer the senses is a gorgeous one, and they seem to compete with one another in the art of degrading their own natures. The stronger, the more famous and the freer an aristocracy has been, the more depraved it will then become. However brilliantly its virtues may once have shone, I dare predict that the splendor of its vices will always outdo them.

The taste for physical gratifications leads a democratic people into no such excesses. There the love of well-being appears as a tenacious, exclusive and universal passion, but its range is narrow. No one thinks of building enormous palaces, of conquering or imitating nature, or of ransacking the world to satisfy one man’s passions. The aim is rather to add a few roods of land to your field, to plant an orchard, to enlarge a house, to keep making life more comfortable and convenient, to avoid trouble, and to meet the smallest needs without effort and almost without cost. These are small objects, but the soul clings to them. It dwells on them closely, day after day, until at last they shut out the rest of the world and sometimes come between the soul and heaven.

It may be said that this applies only to the members of the community who are in humble circumstances, and that wealthier people will show tastes like those they had in aristocratic ages. I deny this. When it comes to physical gratifications, the richest members of a democracy will not show tastes very different from those of the people. Either they rose from the people and truly share those tastes, or they consider it a duty to conform to them. In democratic society the sensuality of the public has taken a moderate and tranquil course, and everyone is bound to follow it. It is as hard to depart from the common rule through one’s vices as through one’s virtues. Rich men who live in democratic nations are therefore more intent on providing for their smallest wants than on extraordinary pleasures. They gratify a host of petty desires without indulging in any great outbursts of passion. They are thus more likely to become enervated than debauched. The particular taste that men of democratic ages have for physical enjoyments is not by nature opposed to the principles of public order. On the contrary, it often needs order in order to be gratified. Nor is it hostile to regularity of morals, for good morals contribute to public tranquillity and favor industry. It may even often be combined with a kind of religious morality. Men want to be as well off as they can in this world without giving up their chance of another. Some physical gratifications cannot be indulged without crime, and from these they strictly abstain. Others are sanctioned by religion and morality, and to these they give up the heart, the imagination and life itself without reserve. In grasping at these lesser gifts, they lose sight of the more precious possessions that make up the glory and greatness of mankind. The reproach I make against the principle of equality is not that it leads men astray in the pursuit of forbidden pleasures, but that it absorbs them entirely in the pursuit of permitted ones. In this way a kind of virtuous materialism may eventually establish itself in the world. It would not corrupt the soul but enervate it, and would silently loosen the springs of its action.
